id: [Were it but Me that gained the Height—]

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

World like a coat, silver clasps, ermine lined, warm with the dead inside, rolling around in the red center—I thought everything had a purpose—this was back when I still drank—and wasn’t I a special traveler, nestled in that pocket amongst the butterscotch candies, the matchbooks? Unessential but accounted for, a steady thing to touch. World like a morning glory, withered every evening, world like a bristling dog, terrified of thunder—I can’t believe how I believed, or how that belief assumed a shape around my body, taking on the imprint of my heat, gaining solidity. When anyone questioned me, I held it forth, let them touch the sleeve—I needed nothing. World like an egret, still and white on the highway divider, world like a regret typed out and then erased—I cannot hold you any closer without everyone seeing, I cannot hold you at all, it seems, your evergreens, your curling potato vine; it’s all too much much, and I a bit of goosedown, a thistle fluff, naked and hatless, unaccounted for and extra, the world like a world like a world.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker once believed that everything in the world had a purpose and that they had a secure place within it.
- The speaker reflects on a past self shaped by drinking, certainty, and a need to feel accounted for.
- The speaker’s former beliefs became tangible and comforting, something they could present to others as proof of stability.
- The speaker now feels unable to hold onto the world or another person without exposure, loss, or overwhelm.
- The poem ends with the speaker feeling fragile, unanchored, and unnecessary in a world that resists clear meaning.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker reflects on a lost sense of purpose and belonging, using cascading metaphors of the world as a coat, flower, animal, bird, and erased regret to trace a movement from belief to exposure. The passage finds that certainty once felt solid but has dissolved into vulnerability and excess, making the self feel unheld and revealing how fragile meaning can be.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: World, Unessential, When

outputs.L1: The world like a coat, with silver clasps and an ermine lining, warm with the dead inside, rolling around in its red center—I thought everything had a purpose—this was back when I still drank—and wasn’t I a special traveler, nestled in that pocket among the butterscotch candies and matchbooks? Unessential, but accounted for; a steady thing to touch. The world like a morning glory, withering every evening; the world like a bristling dog, terrified of thunder—I can’t believe how deeply I believed, or how that belief assumed a shape around my body, taking on the imprint of my heat, gaining solidity. When anyone questioned me, I held it forth, let them touch the sleeve—I needed nothing. The world like an egret, still and white on the highway divider; the world like a regret typed out and then erased—I cannot hold you any closer without everyone seeing. I cannot hold you at all, it seems: your evergreens, your curling potato vine; it’s all too much, too much, and I am a bit of goosedown, a thistle fluff, naked and hatless, unaccounted for and extra, the world like a world like a world.
outputs.L2:
The world was a coat: fastened with silver, lined in ermine, heated by the dead tucked within it, turning in its crimson core. I used to think every single thing meant something—this was in the days when I was still drinking. And didn’t I imagine myself an unusual kind of voyager, curled into that pocket with the butterscotch and the books of matches? Not necessary, maybe, but still counted, still something reliable to put a hand on.

The world was a morning glory, collapsing at dusk. The world was a dog with its hackles up, frightened by thunder. I can hardly believe the way I believed then, or how that faith gathered itself around me, molded to my body’s warmth, and hardened into something real. If someone challenged me, I presented it to them like fabric, invited them to feel the sleeve. I needed nothing.

The world was an egret, motionless and pale on the strip dividing the highway. The world was a remorse written down and deleted. I cannot pull you nearer without making us visible to everyone; in fact, it seems I cannot hold you at all—your evergreens, your twisting potato vine. It is all far too much, and I am only a scrap of goose down, a bit of thistle drift, bare and without a hat, extra, unlisted, while the world remains the world, and the world, and the world.
outputs.L3:
The speaker looks back on a time when the world seemed ordered and purposeful. They once believed that everything had its place and its reason for existing, and that they themselves occupied a secure position within that design. This earlier confidence gave them a sense of belonging, as if their life could be explained and justified by a larger structure.

In reflecting on this past self, the speaker recognizes how much it was shaped by drinking, certainty, and the desire to feel accounted for. Alcohol appears connected to a former way of being: one in which the speaker could feel more fixed, more definite, and perhaps more able to believe in their own importance. Their certainty was not only intellectual but emotional; it helped them feel that they mattered and that their presence in the world had been registered.

Over time, these beliefs became almost tangible. They were not abstract ideas alone, but comforting possessions the speaker could hold onto and even display to others. Their convictions served as evidence of stability, a way of showing that they were grounded, coherent, and safe within the world’s meaning. Belief itself became a kind of proof: proof that the speaker was not lost, not dissolving, not without a place.

In the present, however, that security has fallen away. The speaker no longer feels able to grasp the world or another person without risk. To reach out now means exposure; to love or attach oneself means the possibility of loss; to encounter reality directly means becoming overwhelmed by it. What once felt solid and reassuring now feels unstable, too vast, or too fragile to hold.

By the end of the poem, the speaker is left in a state of vulnerability. They feel delicate, unanchored, and no longer necessary to the world around them. The world does not offer the clear meanings it once seemed to provide, and the speaker cannot recover the old certainty that gave them comfort. Instead, they remain suspended in uncertainty, aware of their own fragility and of a reality that resists being neatly explained.
outputs.L4:
The speaker reflects on a profound loss of purpose, belonging, and certainty. What once seemed stable and protective has begun to fall away, leaving the self exposed to a world that no longer offers clear meaning or reassurance. Through a series of cascading metaphors, the passage imagines the world first as a coat, something that could cover, warm, and contain the speaker. This image suggests that belief once functioned as a kind of shelter: it gave shape to experience and made the speaker feel held.

But that sense of protection does not last. The world is then transformed into a flower, an animal, a bird, and finally into something like an erased regret. Each image shifts the speaker farther away from solidity and closer to fragility, movement, and disappearance. The flower suggests beauty but also perishability; the animal suggests instinct and unpredictability; the bird suggests flight, distance, and the impossibility of being grasped. By the time the passage reaches the image of erased regret, even sorrow itself seems unstable, as if the marks of feeling and memory can be rubbed out.

This progression traces a movement from belief to exposure. The speaker once felt that certainty was firm and reliable, something that could be worn like clothing or inhabited like a home. Now that certainty has dissolved. In its place there is vulnerability, excess, and a sense of being unheld by the structures that once provided meaning. The self is not simply sad; it is overwhelmed by the realization that meaning is far more fragile than it once appeared. The passage therefore becomes a meditation on disillusionment: it shows how easily the world’s apparent coherence can break apart, and how deeply unsettling it is to discover that what once felt solid may have been temporary all along.
outputs.L5:
When the world feels too loud, it becomes easier to confuse what matters with what is merely unessential. We rush through days filled with messages, tasks, and expectations, rarely stopping to ask which of them truly deserve our attention.

The world is full of beauty, but also distraction. It offers us countless things to chase, collect, and worry about. Yet many of these things are unessential. They may seem urgent in the moment, but when we step back, we realize they do not shape who we are or what we value.

When we learn to recognize the unessential, life becomes clearer. We begin to focus on kindness, purpose, connection, and peace. The world does not become simpler, but our place within it does. We understand that not everything demanding our attention deserves our energy.

In the end, wisdom may come from knowing when to let go.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single lyrical prose poem about losing faith in the world, using repeated “World like…” similes and a confessional voice that mentions drinking, grief, and being unaccounted for.
counterfactuals.output: World like a glass left sweating on the table after everyone has gone home. World like a mouth that once promised mercy and now only tastes of coins. I have been drinking again, not enough to disappear, just enough to blur the edges of the room where grief keeps sitting in my chair, wearing my old shirt, answering when someone calls my name. World like a chapel with the candles blown out. World like a dog that no longer comes when called. I used to believe there was a hand beneath things, some bright architecture holding us up, but now the sky looks improvised, the stars pinned there carelessly, the morning arriving with no apology. World like a letter returned unopened. World like a mother turning away in the crowd. I confess I have envied the faithful their clean windows, their bread that means more than bread, their dead gathered tenderly into language. My dead remain dead. My sorrow has no choir. I wake and find myself unaccounted for, absent from every ledger of mercy, a name mislaid by the clerk of dawn. World like a locked house I keep dreaming is mine. World like a river carrying every prayer downstream. Still I stand here, glass in hand, throat full of weather, trying to love what has not loved me back, trying to forgive the dark for being so fluent, trying to say I am here, I was here, though the world keeps passing over me like rain over a stone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal, melancholic paragraph in the style of contemporary literary prose poetry, full of strange images like coats, birds, highways, plants, and small pocket objects.
counterfactuals.output: At dusk the coats return from the highway by themselves, sleeves full of rainwater and the warm bones of absent birds. I stand beside the median where milkweed grows through the cracks like a green alphabet no one living can read, and I empty my pockets onto the asphalt: a bent key, a dead match, a pebble shaped like a sleeping dog, the tiny silver hinge from a door in a dream. Above me, starlings gather in the blue exhaust of evening, rearranging grief into brief, illegible sentences. Every car that passes carries a houseplant in the passenger seat, each leaf pressed to the window as if trying to remember the forest. Somewhere far off, a mother is sewing buttons back onto the sky. Somewhere nearer, my old winter coat hangs from a road sign, turning slowly in the wind, waiting for a body that has forgotten how to come home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental prose poem that begins with “World like a coat” and spirals into themes of belief, intimacy, regret, and the impossibility of holding someone close.
counterfactuals.output:
World like a coat thrown over the shoulders of a sleeping animal,  
warm with borrowed weather, smelling faintly of rain and iron.  
I buttoned it wrong from the beginning. I believed in doors,  
in the alphabet of your spine, in the small cathedral of a cup  
left beside the bed with your lip-print fading from its rim.

To believe is to place a candle inside a mouth and call it singing.  
To love is to mistake the smoke for a hand.

You were there, then not there, then everywhere:  
in the hinge-squeal, in the pear bruising itself sweetly on the counter,  
in the blue vein of morning under the skin of the curtains.  
I said stay as if the word had walls.  
I said mine as if the body were not a river  
practicing departure in every cell.

Once, we lay so close I could hear your thoughts  
turning over like fish beneath ice.  
I wanted to press my ear to the frozen surface forever.  
I wanted to break through.  
Both were forms of damage.

Regret arrives wearing my own face.  
It sits at the foot of the bed and lists the names  
of all the tenderness I mishandled:  
the time I laughed when you were asking to be seen,  
the time I touched you as if touch were proof,  
the time I chose the bright knife of being right  
over the soft bread of being kind.

Forgive me, I say to the room.  
The room, being faithful, keeps its shape.

What god did we make of closeness?  
What altar of clavicle, salt, breath?  
I knelt there. I offered everything:  
my hunger, my fear, the little coins of my childhood,  
my elaborate maps of abandonment.  
Still, you remained you—  
miracle and border, flame behind glass,  
a country whose language I learned just enough to grieve in.

No one can be held. Not really.  
The arms are only parentheses,  
and every beloved sentence eventually leans beyond them.  
Even while you slept against me,  
you were traveling: blood-road, dream-road,  
the dark interior train of the self  
arriving at stations without my name.

I know this now.  
Or almost know it.  
Or believe I know it, which is the human version.

World like a coat, but no one inside it stays warm for long.  
World like a coat I keep reaching to wrap around your shoulders  
after you have crossed the field, after the field has filled with snow,  
after my hands have become two empty rooms  
rehearsing the shape of you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense poetic monologue from the perspective of someone reflecting on sobriety and a former certainty that the world had purpose; make it lush, fragmented, and image-heavy.
counterfactuals.output:
I used to believe the world had a spine.

A bright vertebrae of meaning running under everything — under the butcher’s paper, the rain in the gutters, the moths battering themselves senseless against the porchlight, under my own hungered hands lifting the glass again, again, as if the bottom of it were a chapel bell I could ring with my mouth.

Purpose, I called it.

As if the stars had not simply burned, but written. As if the dead leaves arranged themselves in alleys for me to decipher. As if every bruise was a seal, every fever a visitation, every terrible morning a door with my name cut into it.

I was drunk on more than liquor then. I was drunk on design. On the cathedral grammar of suffering. On the idea that if I hurt beautifully enough, the hurt would turn holy.

And now—

Now I wake clear.

Cruelly clear.

The room arrives without mythology: sock on the floor, glass of water sweating on the crate beside the bed, pale stripe of sun laid across the wall like a hospital bandage. My tongue is my tongue. My hands are only hands. The birds outside are not messengers; they are small engines of feather and need, tearing the morning open because their bodies insist.

Sobriety is not a halo. No.

It is the absence of fog where I expected angels.

It is the sink full of spoons. The unpaid bill. The old shame sitting patiently in its chair, no longer blurred at the edges, no longer transformed into a dragon I could nobly slay. It is hunger with its plain face. Grief without costume. Time without incense.

Some days I miss the grand lie of it — the fever-gold conviction that every ruin was part of a map, that my collapse had architecture, that I was being led by invisible hands through the burning orchard toward some final mercy.

How gorgeous it was, to be doomed with meaning.

How easy, almost, to kneel before disaster if disaster wore a crown.

But the world has taken off its crown.

The world stands bareheaded in the kitchen light, washing a chipped cup, asking nothing of me but this: remain.

Not triumph. Not revelation. Not the trumpet’s silver throat splitting heaven.

Only remain.

Breathe through the minute as it unscrews itself. Touch the table. Name the blue bowl, the cracked tile, the lemon going soft in its yellow skin. Let the afternoon be afternoon and not a prophecy. Let the ache be ache and not a god.

I am learning the animal facts again.

Water enters the body and the body forgives it. Bread is not symbolic when it is bread. Sleep comes sometimes like a tide over black stones. A friend’s voice through the phone can hold you upright for an hour. The heart, that stubborn red engine, does not require a reason to continue, only muscle, only blood, only the next dark pump of itself into itself.

Still, there are evenings—

Yes.

There are evenings when the sky bruises purple over the roofs, and the trees lift their black nets, and for one unbearable second I feel it again: the old certainty hovering at the rim of things, dressed in smoke and honey, whispering that nothing is accidental, not even this ache, not even my white-knuckled refusal, not even the bottles I emptied like little coffins, not even the years I poured away and called an offering.

I almost answer.

I almost say: tell me.

Tell me what it meant.

But the kettle clicks off. A car passes. Somewhere a dog barks itself hoarse at nothing divine.

And I stay.

I stand in the unadorned room of my life, sober as a match before flame, and I do not ask the world to justify me.

This is new.

This is terrifying.

This is the small religion after the great one: not purpose, but presence. Not destiny, but dishes. Not salvation, but the cold water on my wrists, the moon caught in the window like a coin I cannot spend, the body I have dragged back from its glittering edge and must now learn to inhabit without music, without omen, without the sweet black wings of oblivion folding over my eyes.

Maybe meaning was never a road.

Maybe it was the hand on the banister.

The breath after craving.

The morning I did not vanish.

The silence, unscripted, still opening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a one-paragraph prose poem with anaphora, especially the phrase “world like,” blending tenderness, absurdity, grief, and surreal natural imagery.
counterfactuals.output: World like a pear bruised by moonlight, world like a teacup where the ocean keeps forgetting its manners, world like your hand once warm in mine and now a small weather I carry under my ribs. I wake to trees combing their green hair with antlers, to clouds wearing the faces of lost dogs, to a sun that rises sideways as if embarrassed by all it has seen. World like a lullaby sung by a spoon to an empty bowl, world like a cemetery where the flowers gossip in bright, impossible colors, world like the last voicemail blooming moss in the dark cupboard of my phone. I want to be gentle with everything: the cracked egg of morning, the snail towing its silver cathedral, the ridiculous stars stapled crookedly above us. World like a whale asleep in a walnut shell, world like a mother calling from another room that no longer has walls, world like grief putting on its little red boots and stepping carefully through the puddles of my heart. Still, the rain strokes the roofs; still, the foxgloves lift their purple bells to no one and ring.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
